verses.text: Joseph fell on his father’s face, wept on him, and kissed him.
Joseph commanded his servants, the physicians, to embalm his father; and the physicians embalmed Israel.
Forty days were fulfilled for him, for that is how many the days it takes to embalm. The Egyptians wept for him for seventy days.
When the days of weeping for him were past, Joseph spoke to the house of Pharaoh, saying, “If now I have found favor in your eyes, please speak in the ears of Pharaoh, saying,

‘My father made me swear, saying, “Behold, I am dying. Bury me in my grave which I have dug for myself in the land of Canaan.” Now therefore, please let me go up and bury my father, and I will come again.’”
Pharaoh said, “Go up, and bury your father, just like he made you swear.”
Joseph went up to bury his father; and with him went up all the servants of Pharaoh, the elders of his house, all the elders of the land of Egypt,
All the house of Joseph, his brothers, and his father’s house. Only their little ones, their flocks, and their herds, they left in the land of Goshen.
There went up with him both chariots and horsemen. It was a very great company.
They came to the threshing floor of Atad, which is beyond the Jordan, and there they lamented with a very great and severe lamentation. He mourned for his father seven days.

When the inhabitants of the land, the Canaanites, saw the mourning in the floor of Atad, they said, “This is a grievous mourning by the Egyptians.” Therefore its name was called Abel Mizraim, which is beyond the Jordan.
His sons did to him just as he commanded them,

for his sons carried him into the land of Canaan, and buried him in the cave of the field of Machpelah, which Abraham bought with the field, for a possession of a burial site, from Ephron the Hittite, before Mamre.
Joseph returned into Egypt — he, and his brothers, and all that went up with him to bury his father, after he had buried his father.
When Joseph’s brothers saw that their father was dead, they said, “It may be that Joseph will hate us, and will fully pay us back for all the evil which we did to him.”
They sent a message to Joseph, saying, “Your father commanded before he died, saying,

‘You shall tell Joseph, “Now please forgive the disobedience of your brothers, and their sin, because they did evil to you.”’ Now, please forgive the disobedience of the servants of the God of your father.” Joseph wept when they spoke to him.
His brothers also went and fell down before his face; and they said, “Behold, we are your servants.”
Joseph said to them, “Don’t be afraid, for am I in the place of God?
As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good, to bring to pass, as it is today, to save many people alive.
Now therefore don’t be afraid. I will nourish you and your little ones.” He comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.
Joseph lived in Egypt, he, and his father’s house. Joseph lived one hundred ten years.
Joseph saw Ephraim’s children to the third generation. The children also of Machir, the son of Manasseh, were born on Joseph’s knees.
Joseph said to his brothers, “I am dying, but God will surely visit you, and bring you up out of this land to the land which he swore to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob.”
Joseph took an oath of the children of Israel, saying, “God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here.”
So Joseph died, being one hundred ten years old, and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt.

footnotes.content: Joseph falls and weeps over his father's face—the man he'd once feared has become his treasure. Love makes our losses visible, and grief is the price we pay for having loved well. This is a son honoring the father God gave him.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Egyptian physicians: Joseph honors his father with the customs of the land that sheltered them both. Even in death, Jacob receives the dignity of Egypt's care, a sign that Joseph has earned not just Pharaoh's favor but his trust.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty days and seventy days—Egypt mourns a foreign shepherd as if he were pharaoh's own. When godly character touches a people, they recognize something worth honoring, even across the border between strangers and kin.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph waits until grief softens before he speaks. Wisdom knows when words will land. His request—to honor his father's deathbed oath—is both practical and tender, the language of a man who's learned how to ask.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Machpelah in Canaan—the family tomb, the land of promise. Joseph reminds Pharaoh of an oath to the dying, a claim every human heart understands. The dead deserve to be kept; promises deserve to be honored.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Pharaoh's consent is swift. A ruler who sees virtue in his servant grants what virtue requests. This is authority used rightly—to protect what matters most to those who've served faithfully.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A procession of servants and elders—Egypt itself escorts the patriarch home. Joseph's station lifts his father's funeral into a state ceremony, a son's way of saying: this man meant everything.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The whole family travels, but the little ones stay behind in Goshen—safe, known land. Even in grief, Joseph thinks like a father, like a steward who won't leave the young unguarded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Chariots and horsemen: the funeral has become a pilgrimage of power and presence. The show of force is not prideful here—it's reverence, the language Egypt speaks when something sacred moves through it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The threshing floor of Atad, beyond the Jordan—a place known to shepherds, a place of labor. Seven days of mourning: Joseph gives his father the mourning a son owes, public and unhurried, claiming space to grieve.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Abel Mizraim—'meadow of Egypt,' the Canaanites remember. The name marks the place: here Egypt grieved deeply for one of ours. Landmark names hold memory; this ground witnessed that a foreigner could be loved like family.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: His sons obeyed his command—the deathbed wish becomes the living law. Honoring the dying is how we keep faith with the covenant they carried; it's how the next generation learns what love costs.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Machpelah, the cave Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite—Jacob rests where the covenant began, in the field of promise. Each generation adds a body to that cave; each affirms the promise is still true.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph returns to Egypt—his home now, his post, his calling. The funeral complete, he heads back to the life God gave him. This is faithfulness: honoring the past, then stepping forward into the day ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph's brothers are still afraid. They think the debt unpaid—old wounds can whisper louder than new mercies. Fear asks: will he remember what we did? Will kindness run out when the man who restrained it is gone?
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They craft a message, invoke a deathbed wish they may or may not have secured. Sometimes we approach mercy through layers of caution, as if honesty alone won't hold us up. Fear makes us indirect.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They ask forgiveness for disobedience and sin—the plain words for what they did. Joseph weeps at their plea. Confession unlocks something in him; there is grace waiting on the other side of admitting what was wrong.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They prostrate themselves: 'We are your servants.' The bow echoes their childhood cruelty—the theft, the pit, the sale. But now submission is willing, an act of trust offered to a brother who chose not to become what they feared.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph asks: 'Am I in the place of God?' The question holds the whole truth of forgiveness—he is a man, not judge; God alone settles the accounts. To forgive is to step out of that seat and let God have it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: What you meant for evil, God meant for good—the turning point of Genesis itself. The pit, the slavery, the years of hiding: God was remaking it all into the salvation of a family and a people. Not all harm becomes good; but God's purpose cannot be stopped by it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph nourishes them, speaks kindly—more than forgiveness, he moves toward them with care. The brothers' children will eat bread Joseph provides; they will learn forgiveness lived out in daily loyalty. This is mercy that lasts.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: One hundred ten years in Egypt—a full, long life given to a foreign land and a pharaoh's court. Yet Joseph's heart remained fixed on Canaan. Length of days is a blessing; where they're spent shapes who we become.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Grandchildren and great-grandchildren grew on his knees—the bond between generations, preserved. Joseph saw the promise multiplying, not just in words but in faces, in a family that would inherit the covenant he guarded.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: On his deathbed, Joseph points toward Canaan: 'God will surely visit you and bring you up.' Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Joseph—each keeper of the promise, each died in faith, seeing it from afar. This is how trust passes down.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Carry my bones from here—Joseph binds his children to the promise with an oath. Even in death, he testifies: Egypt is not home. The promised land is worth the weight of carrying him there.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Joseph dies and is embalmed—the book of Genesis closes with a body, not a grave, waiting. Readers today hear an echo: his faith outlasted his years. Centuries later, his bones did travel home, carried by hands that held his oath as sacred. What we trust God for, He finishes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
